chunks: What a thermal relief pad is. The question: What is a thermal relief pad?
A thermal relief connects a pad to a copper plane through a few narrow spokes, with a gap around the rest of the pad. It exists for soldering.
A big plane soaks up heat, so a pad tied solidly to it may never get hot enough for solder to flow. The spokes slow the heat loss but keep the electrical connection.
The price is more resistance and less current capacity.
Imagine heating a small cup welded to a huge cold metal sheet. The sheet pulls the heat away as fast as you add it. Now attach the cup with a few thin wire links instead.
The cup heats quickly and is still attached. The sheet is the plane; the links are the spokes.
Left, the pad is merged into the pour and the plane drains heat from the whole circumference.
Right, the pad is separated by a clearance ring and joined only through four spokes, so soldering heat is mostly confined to the pad and the barrel, while the electrical connection remains.
The pad (darker disc) is the same size in both.
Spoke: one of the narrow copper bridges joining the pad to the plane.
Thermal resistance: how many degrees of difference it takes to push one watt of heat through something, in K/W. Cold joint: a weak solder joint that never got hot enough to bond.
Tombstoning: a small part standing up on one end after soldering, because one pad melted first ("Skinny vs thick traces and shapes").
Exposed thermal pad: a pad under a power chip meant to carry heat out ("Reducing component heating on the board").

2 amps at a 20 degrees Celsius rise. That is the whole idea.
"A thermal relief connects a pad to a plane or pour through a few narrow spokes with a gap around the rest of the pad.
It limits how fast heat leaves the pad during soldering so the joint reaches temperature and doesn't cold-solder or tombstone, and rework is easier.
The cost is higher electrical and thermal resistance and less current, so I use it on ordinary pins and turn it off on high-current or thermal pads."
